children: As Americans brace for the outcome to next week’s midterm elections, a potential shift in power could shape the U.S. trucking industry as issues such as broker liability, driver certification, and U.S. trade policy are up for grabs in the 2027-2028 legislative session.

The trucking industry encompasses everything from third-party logistics providers, less-than-truckload shippers, final-mile transports, and full truckload carriers, all of whom have a unique stake in the outcome of the election.

According to Drivewyze, the trucking industry employs ~13% of the U.S. labor force and moves two-thirds of domestic freight. The industry is regulated on the federal level by the Department of Transportation, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and Transportation Safety Administration (TSA).

While the Republican Party held a majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, the trucking industry enjoyed a pro-business administration with a light regulatory touch. Coupled with the recent crack-down on non-English speaking or unauthorized truck drivers, compliant trucking companies have enjoyed reduced industry capacity and higher shipping rates.

The American Trucking Association (ATA), the industry’s leading voice in Washington, does not endorse either political party but rather supports lawmakers who favor federal and state limits on large commercial vehicle lawsuits and accident fraud, expanded urban and highway truck parking infrastructure, and favorable labor and driver rules.

“The decisions made in Washington don’t stay in Washington. They affect how we operate, how we invest, and how we serve our customers every day,” said ATA Chairman Derek Leathers, chairman, and CEO of Werner Enterprises
“Our industry needs a strong, unified voice at the table to make sure policymakers understand those realities and fight for policies that enable trucking to keep America moving.”
The way Congress leans and the regulatory environment for the trucking business hinges on the outcome at the polls on November 3.

According to research firm Armstrong & Associates, if Republicans continue to hold the House and Senate, current regulatory policies will likely remain intact with broker liability reform passing under President Trump’s conditions. This would be bullish for carriers with in-house brokerages, including Knight-Swift
, as well as well-capitalized third-party logistics companies that can absorb higher insurance rates, such as C.H. Robinson Worldwide

If Congress is split between the two parties, the trucking industry can expect to see more oversight of tariffs (though policy remains with the Executive branch) and new laws from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (agency under the Department of Transportation).

Following the Supreme Court’s decision on broker liability (Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport), freight brokers have been advocating for a federal standard regarding broker liability. Should a Democratic-controlled Congress pass the responsibility to states, brokers will have to adapt to state-by-state laws that will further complicate the industry and leave smaller brokers more vulnerable to stricter state regulations.

Besides the overall control of the House and Senate, certain key Senate races across the country will also be closely watched by industry, including the outcome in Maine (Susan Collins R-Maine), Alaska (Dan Sullivan R-Alaska), and Ohio (John Husted R-Ohio), the three of which have supported legislation that governs language requirements for drivers, relaxes scheduling restrictions, and adjustments to EPA emission regulations for cold-weather states.

In the House, Kevin Hern (R-Okla), Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), and Mike Collins (R-Ga) are all hoping to hold onto their seats and keep favorable trucking regulations (or the lack of new regulations) intact.

Ultimately, the midterm elections could prove consequential for an industry already navigating shifting capacity, higher operating costs, and evolving federal regulations. For the trucking industry, the balance of power in Washington could help determine whether the next two years bring regulatory relief or a new layer of compliance and cost pressures.

title: The industry that keeps America moving now waits to see how America votes
